Prologue: Narrative: A Central Organizer of Lived Experience

Joe Caruso

Joe Caruso

Joe Caruso   CONTACT Joe Caruso Joe@carusoleadership.com Caruso Leadership Institute, 26561 W. River Road, Grosse Ile, MI 48138.

Narrative is the Rosetta Stone of the mind. It is the quintessential formation for the foundation of self, thought, self/other, and therefore all other considerations.

It is at once, this simple and this complex: A single thought cannot exist for any length of time in singularity in-and-of-itself alone, without being connected to another thought. This is not an unnecessary compulsion. It is how the mind creates meaning.

The need for the mind to create connection is the genesis and conception of meaning. The connections continue, followed by more thoughts and feelings and the mind develops and deepens a story around the original notion. This is narrative.

While we have many stories in our lives, our self-narrative is our foundational narrative. It is the story by which we determine what all else means. It drives affect, love, likes and dislikes, proclivities, hobbies, salaries, jobs, familial relationships, and even dinner conversations.

The simplest example I can think of to illustrate how self-narrative drives meaning is to consider the notion of a deer. If you love the graceful and generally peaceful animal and find it to be a thing of beauty, you may be an animal lover or nature-loving individual. If you find it to be a very expensive and an invasive pest, you may like nature, but that deer may also be eating every flower you plant. If you define the deer as wild game or venison, you may be a hunter or a chef. If you define the same deer as the most dangerous and deadly animal for humans, you may just live in rural Michigan (because deer crossing the road cause accidents every day in this region).

Our foundational narrative can be apparent to us or partially, mostly or fully hidden from us. Narratives are fully and presently in every thought we have nonetheless. Therefore, the understanding of narrative is necessarily critical to analytic work.

This idea takes nothing away from theories of construct of the mind, the existence and power of transference and countertransference or schools of analytical thought from Freud to Klein to Kohut.

Epilogue: Narrative: A Central Organizer of Lived Experience

Joe Caruso

Joe Caruso

Joe Caruso   CONTACT Joe Caruso Joe@carusoleadership.com Caruso Leadership Institute, 26561 W. River Road, Grosse Ile, MI 48138.

I would like to close the idea of Narrative as the Central Organizer of a Lived Experience with some additional thoughts.

Narrative is not new. It has driven minds, lives, thoughts, behaviors, and even religions since humankind began. Narrative can shift across cultures and across centuries. As narrative shifts in a new culture and new time and even in a new life, the old narrative remnants may remain. History shows how a culture from 4,000 years ago can drive a religious narrative today. From ancient Egypt to Greek mythology, to the Roman Empire and Asian cultures, narratives are passed down across cultures and times. Consider what the journey through the underworld of The Egyptian intermediary period and the western idea of purgatory have in common. Remnants remain. Consider the idea in ancient Egypt of an afterlife where you can be reunited with friends and family and the western idea of heaven. Remnants remain. Narrative can be generational; families within cultures. Shawn’s apple story demonstrated this notion — how a narrative can be driven or dragged across a generation over time — unknowingly and unconsciously — and only through awareness and examination does it significantly change. From narratives of a spiritual nature — those considered special or untouchable — to those of a generational and personal nature, narrative is not new but it can become new.

Whether we consider a culture of one (e.g., an individual mind) or a culture of many (e.g., a collective mind), life can be described as a journey of narratives that cling, or are clung to, and narratives that are replaced. But narrative itself ever exists. It ever exists because it is the central organizer of the mind.

Part of my work is determining and understanding the narrative of an organization and helping leaders create fundamental and substantial change. This isn’t skills training. It’s not about learning what to do and how to do it. It is literally changing the foundational context of how an organization understands itself and learns to adapt a new driving narrative that better serves them as individuals and as a collective.

David and Goliath: What If He Loses?

J. Hoffmann MD

J. Hoffmann

J. Hoffmann   J. Miguel Hoffmann, M.D., is full member of the IPA (International Psycho-Analytic Association), part time in clinical practice. Honorary President of the Argentine Branch of WAIMH, serving on the WAIMH Board 1989–2000. For 25 years Director of a Center for Research and Prevention in Early Childhood, working for 10 years (2006–2015) full time in the Community in preventive practices, both with Government and NGOs.CONTACT J. Miguel Hoffmann, M.D. miguel.hoffmann@gmail.com Juncal 4690, Rio 3°-3, CABA, (1425), Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Infant’s volition has not been explored in healthy development. Our research conducted on the environmental response to infant’s initiatives (Hoffmann, Popbla, and Duhalde, 1998) shows that maternal attitude has a direct correlation with successful development of initiatives in infants aged 4 to 12 months, having implications for the capacities of infants to unfold as much as endowments allow. The opposite also is true. Infants who are more thwarted in the development of their potential initiatives show greater reactivity and conflict in early relationships with the caregiver, impacting the development of a healthy self. These claims will be discussed with proposals made in recent decades by some authors who have focused on the coming together of a self in the first year of life. The ramifications of this early start in one’s life can be credited to Lou Sander, whom we honor in this issue. Sander was gifted with a capacity to see with a “relational eye” and to state it in everyday language, while simultaneously using very sophisticated inventions to validate his assumptions. This work has made it possible to solve the riddle of the David and Goliath story that is part of the miracle of life over death, of love over hate, of health over sickness, which makes (most) mothers able to become good enough or whatever defines a progressive meeting between the infant’s doings with the doings of mothers.

Feminine Issues and the Relational Turn: “The Girls Deserve More Respect”

Joye Weisel-Barth Ph.D., Psy.D.

Joye Weisel-Barth

Joye Weisel-Barth   Joye Weisel-Barth, Ph.D., Psy.D., is a senior instructor, training analyst, and supervisor at the Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis in Los Angeles. She teaches courses in Basic Analytic Concepts, Freud, Interpersonal Psychoanalysis, Neuroscience, Attachment Theory, and Varieties of Relational Psychoanalysis. Joye is Book Review Editor for Psychoanalysis, Self and Context, Associate Editor of Psychoanalytic Dialogues, and a frequent contributor to major psychoanalytic journals. Her analytic practice is in Encino, California, and she loves her doggies.CONTACT Joye Weisel-Barth, Ph.D., Psy.D. dr.joye@sbcglobal.net 4826 Andasol Avenue, Encino, CA 91316.

The second wave of feminism deserves recognition for its contribution to the relational ethos. I suggest that the feminist contribution to psychoanalysis has been part of a larger cultural shift toward equality, connectedness, and increased attention to human stories about real-life experiences, including trauma. In addition to expanding the ranks of analysts, women have challenged the field to examine and modify libido theory, its power alignments, and the clinical roles available to the analyst. In the clinical case, I seek to convey a feminist sensibility—rather than a program. This sensibility embodies many maternal qualities, such as concerned listening, affect attunement, mentalization, openness to the unknown, and the attribution of seriousness and meaning to the suffering other.

Part II offers an understanding of how unusual, creative, and meaningful the course taught at the Chicago Institute is. Chapter 1 explains how the course came into existence and outlines its structure, along with giving a syllabus for the course. Chapter 2 is probably the essence of this issue of the journal, as it gives detailed student responses to the analysts’ presentations. Chapter 3 details the student responses to one class in particular, a special class on Allen Siegel’s book, Heinz Kohut and the Psychology of the Self, at Allen’s house in which he addresses questions raised by the students about the book in particular and self psychology in general.

Chapter 1: The Origin and Structure of the Course

Marcia Dobson PHD and John Riker PHD

John Riker

John Riker   John H. Riker, Ph.D., is a professor of Philosophy at Colorado College. He is the author of four books interrelating psychoanalysis and philosophy, especially ethics. He is a member of the International Association of Psychoanalytic Self Psychology and a co-chair of APsaA’s Committee on Psychoanalysis and Undergraduate Education.John H. Riker, Ph.D. jriker@coloradocollege.edu Department of Philosophy, Colorado College, 14 E. Cache la Poudre, Colorado Springs, CO 80903.

Origin

Who knows where ideas come from that sprout and burgeon into exciting adventures with equally magnificent results? In this case, Marcia had just invented a psychoanalysis minor at Colorado College, after having received her second Ph.D. in Clinical Psychology (the first was in Classical Philology), primarily because she saw a dearth of any psychoanalytic theory in the Psychology Department’s predominantly cognitive and behavioral curriculum. It then occurred that her husband and Professor of Philosophy, John Riker, at the invitation of Jonathan Lear, became the Kohut Professor at the University of Chicago in the fall of 2003. During that semester, he gave a public lecture on “The Life of the Soul,” which he was also invited (by Arnold Goldberg) to give to the Chicago meeting of self-psychologists, at which time we had the chance to meet, among others, Marian Tolpin, Sallie Jenkins, Ernest Wolf, David Terman, Allen Siegel, and many other talented and intelligent self psychologists. We also attended a “Meet the Author” program at the Psychoanalytic Institute and were amazed at the originality and depth of ideas we were hearing. When we returned home, Marcia longingly expressed the wish that we could have these exceptionally gifted people come to speak at Colorado College for our psychoanalysis minor. But we both understood that this would be much too expensive. Then John said: “Well, if we can’t bring them here, why don’t we go to them?” There followed a phone call to David Terman, at this point Director of the Institute, a meeting with his colleagues on the Board, and it was done! That simple! And so, in 2007 the course came into existence.

It has been 11 years now since we have been bringing our Colorado College students to the Chicago Psychoanalytic Institute in the summer for a course lasting for a month or so, which we have entitled “Contemporary Psychoanalysis: Theory and Practice.” Almost 200 students have taken the course or a second course we added for several years, “Psychoanalysis, Culture, and Society.” Students interact with as many as 15 analysts in 17 days—analysts who give their time to come to discuss their recent writing, present case studies or vignettes, or, really, talk about whatever they choose to, including talking about their careers in psychoanalysis.

Marcia Dobson PHD and John Riker PHD

John Riker

John Riker   John H. Riker, Ph.D. jriker@coloradocollege.edu Department of Philosophy, Colorado College, 14 E. Cache la Poudre, Colorado Springs, CO 80903.

At the end of each class, we ask students to write either an annotated bibliographic essay on a psychoanalytic subject of their choosing or a short paper. We include here three examples of the kind of work we receive. The first is an annotated bibliography written by Monica Black, a drama major, who has been “play-acting” since childhood and who is now a serious actress, exploring the question of “Why Perform?” She wrote the paper when she was a sophomore. The second is written by Becca Stine, a junior creative writing major, who, when she saw Waiting for Godot at the Chicago Shakespeare Theater, had moving insights about her relation with her sister, insights that were enhanced by the psychoanalytic reading we did in relation to the drama. The third, by first-year neuroscience major Peter Lehman, is an annotated bibliography that seeks to understand how neurobiology and psychoanalysis can best intersect.

Chapter 2: To the Lighthouse and the Oedipal Triangle: Impotence, Erotic Degradation, and the Oedipus Complex from Freudian and Self-Psychological Perspectives

Caroline Beaton

Caroline Beaton

Caroline Beaton   Caroline Beaton graduated from Colorado College in 2013 with a major in English and a minor in Psychoanalysis. She is currently a freelance journalist and documentarian based in Boulder, Colorado.CONTACT Caroline Beaton caroline@carolinebeaton.com 225 S. Broadway, PO Box 9777, Denver, CO 80223.

This article seeks to understand the Ramsay family in To the Lighthouse (Woolf, 1927) from both Freudian and Kohutian self-psychological models. I specifically address the Oedipus conflict and erotic degradation dynamics as a means to explore the broader phenomena of psychical impotence and disintegration. Ultimately, this article reveals that Freud’s understanding of psychical impotence and Kohut’s notion of disintegration are 2 sides of the same coin. Accordingly, a broader, intermediary theoretical understanding of the Oedipal Triangle and its effects is needed.

Narrative as a Mode of Knowing

Daniel Goldin Psy.D.

Daniel Goldin

Daniel Goldin   Daniel Goldin, Psy.D., is a psychoanalyst practicing in South Pasadena, California. He serves as an associate editor of Psychoanalytic Inquiry and on the editorial board of Psychoanalysis: Self and Context. He has written articles for Psychoanalytic Dialogues, The International Journal of Psychoanalytic Self Psychology, and Psychoanalytic Inquiry.CONTACT Daniel Goldin, Psy.D. daniel@danielgoldinpractice.com 1515 Hope Street, Suite 202, South Pasadena, CA 91030.

Thinkers over the millenium have detected two styles or modes of knowing, although they have used different words to categorize these modes. Medieval Christian scholastics distinguished between knowing by reason and knowing by faith or revelation. Kohut distinguished between knowing by empirical observation and knowing by empathic immersion. Similarly, the cognitive psychologist Jerome Bruner proposed two ways of knowing: a paradigmatic mode of knowing and a narrative mode of knowing. The paradigmatic mode we know well from the natural sciences. It involves creating predictive models or laws. The narrative mode concerns itself with the motivated reasons for exceptional occurrences and recruits the faculty of empathy. This article jumps off of Bruner’s distinction between these two ways of knowing and argues that narrative is the preeminent mode in psychoanalysis. In the process, I make a distinction between narrative and empathy. The narrative mode requires empathy but it isn’t the same as empathy. Stories transcend our individual subjectivities by connecting different minds, different places and different times. We put ourselves in the grip of a story in order to know more than we can know when we are not in its grip.

The Conscious and Unconscious Procedures, Motives and Meanings of Pre-Pubescent Problem Sexual Behavior

Gerard Webster Ph.D., Psy.D.

Gerard Webster

Gerard Webster   Gerard P. Webster, Ph.D., Psy.D., is Supervising and Training Psychoanalyst, and Forensic and Counselling Psychologist, affiliated with the Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis, Los Angeles.CONTACT Gerard P. Webster, Ph.D., Psy.D. gerard@gerardwebster.com Studio 33, Level 3, 8 Hill Street, Surry Hills, NSW 2010, Australia.

Research into the sexual behavior of children remains in its infancy despite growing awareness that, under certain circumstances, it can at times be harmful to those involved. Of the research undertaken thus far, much has focused on descriptive data (Who did what to whom? What is the age difference between the children involved? How many times did they do it?). Little or no research or theorizing has been directed to the questions of “why it occurred” and “what it means” to the children involved. This article examines the cases of 2 boys whose sexual behaviors with other children were found to be problematic by child protection authorities. By considering the transference-countertransference relationship in the treatment setting with each of these boys, it is argued that an examination of the conscious and unconscious procedures, motives and meanings of such children, expands professional horizons of understanding about the phenomenon of pre-pubescent problem sexual behavior. This arrticle concludes that research, particularly through the lens of contemporary psychoanalysis, has much to offer clinicians who assess and provide treatment to children whose sexual behaviors fall outside the normal range.

Chapter 1: Why Perform?

Monica Black

Monica Black

Monica Black   Monica Black, originally from Chicago, graduated from Colorado College in 2019 with a major in Psychology. She currently works with foster children in Colorado Springs.CONTACT Monica Black M_black@coloradocollege.edu 512 E. San Miguel Street, Colorado Springs, CO 80903.

It has been said by Marlon Brando’s friends and family that the first time he ever performed, he pretended to be the pigs and cows that populated his family farm to get his alcoholic mother’s attention. The list of classical actors with despair-laden childhoods goes on: Humphrey Bogart’s penny-hoarding parents never kissed the boy; Ingrid Bergman grew up motherless and was shuttled from home to home, all the time refusing to take off her mother’s clothes; Katharine Hepburn found her beloved older brother hanged and celebrated his birthday as her own for years. These traumatic losses might lead one to believe that the actor’s abilities formed as an adaptation to compensate for a narcissistic vulnerability, that the desire for attention and validation (Kohutian mirroring) becomes satisfied by the applause that one receives. But my sense is that the motivation to act consists of more than being applauded for balancing a ball on one’s nose for treats. It is the longing to transform the self that plays the central role.

It is my intention in this bibliography to uncover what self-psychology can tell us about the art of acting, specifically. (Although related, the arts of acting, directing, designing, and appreciating the theater are driven by distinct psychological impulses; directing and designing are much more like the visual arts than acting, which exists in the body and its reference to itself.) My question is why, exactly, the creative nature of an individual turns to acting as the artistic outlet. My claim is that acting, in particular, allows young actors to identify with another, missing part of themselves.

As someone with an impulse to perform and knowing my own history quite well, I first explore my own childhood. As a child I lived in my head; I read and I played. Most of my fantasies revolved around victimhood. My favorite book was A Tree Grows in Brooklyn, by Betty Smith (2006). I wished the life that Frankie lived was mine, from the days that she sold tin cans for pennies with her kid brother until she was a secretary in a law firm in pencil skirts. In one common recess game, Ferocious Doggy, the title character did everything in his power to hunt the poor, helpless little kittens, played by me and a dear friend. The dog occasionally got close, and he would put us in jail (a grate in the asphalt) to eat later, but we were freed by a benevolent recurring character, the sometimes absent but always heroic father of the two kittens. If memory serves me, we played this game every day for an entire year. It was only in our maturity that we stopped.

Enactment as Unconscious Communication

Caroline Polmear

Caroline Polmear

Caroline Polmear   Caroline Polmear is a Training and Supervising Psychoanalyst of the British Psychoanalytical Society and Institute.CONTACT Caroline Polmear caroline.polmear@btinternet.com 10 Grand Avenue, Muswell Hill, London, N10 3BB, United Kingdom.

I explore the way in which unconscious primitive and nonsymbolic experience is communicated to the analyst’s unconscious through enactment. As the analyst receives the projections unconsciously, she is encouraged to enact aspects of the patient’s internal world. The analytic work then is through the understanding of these subtle and ubiquitous enactments. I value the work of understanding enactments as a rich and subtle pathway into the deepest levels of the patient’s unconscious. I explore the nature of this work and illustrate my point with clinical examples.

On his shoulders have stood many of the foremost thinkers in development and psychoanalysis.

This issue continues to explore his contributions and their influence on subsequent clinicians, theorists, and researchers. Prologue: Relational Turn: How and Why It Happened

Daniel Goldin Psy.D.

Daniel Goldin

Daniel Goldin   CONTACT Daniel Goldin, Psy.D. daniel@danielgoldinpractice.com 1515 Hope Street, Suite 202, South Pasadena, CA 91030.

Freud imagined the human animal as originating in an autistic, isolated phase and moving to a more mature phase of relations to others. In his second-to-last book, Mitchell (2014) reversed the equation. “Human minds are fundamentally social phenomena,” he wrote, “that become focalized and secondarily elaborated by individuals” (p. xii). He used the word relationality throughout this book and even crowned the book with that title. This turning of the adjective relational into the abstract noun relationality is a telling feature of the relational movement in the new millennium. Fairburn’s (1952) famous, tentative notion that “libido is object seeking” (p. 78) has turned into an all-encompassing credo. We don’t just behave in relation to others: The world we live in is suffused with the quality of such relating. Relationality, as with Freud’s reality, is the very condition of being human, our initial and forever state of nature, what we get to when the veils fall from our eyes. This is a gigantic shift from the disengaged stance favored by post-enlightenment thinkers from Descartes to Darwin to Freud, philosophers who offered, as Nagel (1986) put it, “a view from nowhere.” For most contemporary psychoanalysts, Freud’s vaunted reality and our emotional transactions with those closest to us can never be fully disambiguated, hence the need for a new word that describes both conditions simultaneously.

The idea that the theater of operations in psychoanalysis is constituted by two mutually influencing minds, as opposed to one mind observed by a neutral cognitive apparatus, has become not just acceptable, but axiomatic. It was not always so. Kohut and Sullivan, who tilled the soil from opposite ends of the field, developed their ideas in exile from mainstream institutes. Mitchell, Ghent, and Bass started Psychoanalytic Dialogues as a way to disseminate relational ideas considered too heretical for mainstream publications. Psychoanalytic Dialogues is currently the most widely read psychoanalytic journal in the field, and it is hard now to find a reputable author in the psychoanalytic world who still cleaves to a one-person psychology (a problem confronted by the editor of this issue as he sought a counter view).

The writers of this issue grapple with the sources of a new status quo in psychoanalysis, one in which relationality, however one defines the term exactly, has replaced reality as a condition of being and as an endpoint of understanding. Each writes a how-so story of this status quo. The challenge for each author has been to relationalize the relational point of view, which has become less a point of view than an atmosphere.

I see roughly two modes in which the writers in this issue grapple with their task. The first is an autobiographical/philosophical mode, in which the author looks back to a time when he/she struggled with established classical (or interpersonal) ideas to arrive at a more relational sensibility. Stolorow, Stern, and McKay by way of Jessica Benjamin, operate predominantly in this mode. The emphasis is on the author’s own changing experience as he/she engages with patients and experiments with new relational frameworks to explain unique happenings. The second is a sociopolitical mode, in which the author considers forces in the culture that shaped the new outlook or made it conceivable. This group is further divided roughly into those who see relationality as an emancipatory response to oppressive hegemonic cultural influences (Harris, Seligman), for whom Foucault is as important a forebear as Sullivan or Kohut, and those who see relationality as emerging from new creative tendrils in new subcultures (Weisel-Barth).

Christina Emanuel steps outside the constraints of the issue to consider the relational turn from the perspective of one who never felt it as a turn. For Emanuel, the turn, which most of the authors in this issue experienced as a skeptical questioning of authority, has become an authoritative way that, itself, discourages questioning simply by having rendered most of its old adversaries irrelevant. Skepticism needs an establishment to press up against. In the end, Emanuel’s critique of the relational tradition squares with the self-questioning, countertransference-valuing nature of the tradition itself.

In Memoriam: Harriet J. Pappenheim

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Two years ago Harriet Pappenheim sent Joe Lichtenberg and me a note that an issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry devoted to clinical examples of unconscious communication would be timely and valuable to stimulate attention to this ubiquitous clinical phenomena. She would be happy to edit an issue. So, this became one of her professional contributions.

She died in the middle of the preparation of the issue. She has been a valuable contributing editor and we miss her greatly. The remainder of this memorandum was written by Harriet herself.

Harriet Pappenheim was a well-known couple, family, and individual therapist who had a private practice for many years, with an additional specialty in family business relationship counseling. She was featured on national radio and in national newspaper articles and appeared on TV shows like Good Morning America and The Today Show. She authored Bringing Home the Bacon (Harper Collins), which was later published in paperback as For Richer or Poorer: Keeping Your Marriage Happy When She’s Making More Money. Harriet was an original founder and director of the Parent’s Center in New York City. She organized, produced, and participated in over 20 professional scientific conferences in New York City and also wrote and presented numerous scientific papers to therapists and other professionals—nationally and internationally—on psychotherapy, psychoanalysis, and couple therapy. She co-edited this psychoanalytic journal and was on the Editorial Board of Psychoanalytic Inquiry.

The articles in this issue were presented at an Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis (ICP) Symposium that took place on February 20, 2015, in Los Angeles, California. The meeting was conceptualized and sponsored by the then current candidates of, and recent graduates from, the ICP in Los Angeles. Entitled “Complexity and the Relational Unconscious: A Symposium for and by the ICP Community,” the program represented for all of us candidates and recent candidates, “a field of dreams.”

The idea for this program emerged organically from conversations among members of the Long Distance Committee of ICP. This committee was comprised of candidates and recent graduates of ICP’s Weekend Program for Psychoanalytic Training, and included current and former candidates representing five different states in the United States, as well as Australia. Within less than 2 months from the original “Call for Papers” soliciting submissions from current candidates and recent graduates, 33 fully completed papers were received.

As is premised in complexity theory, when a system arrives at a tipping point, the system itself morphs into new ways of being in the world, and something quite unexpected and unpredictable happens. So, it seems that in this systemwide effort to hold an ICP symposium, unanticipated innovations from candidates and recent graduates crossed that threshold. Although one’s candidacy may well be the most thoughtful and creative time in a prospective analyst’s career, as demonstrated here by the rapid response to the call for papers, frequently a lack of self confidence in the candidate can impede such efforts to consolidate and share ideas. In this case, the proposed symposium provided both motivation and opportunity for the ICP population, demonstrating that when encouraged, independent thought can yield abundant results.

One theme that emerged in the papers that were presented in the symposium was a sense of freedom; that is, there emerged an exhilarating release from false binaries and artificial boundaries in theory and practice that have so often constrained the field. Instead, the emphasis in these presentations was on the fluid dimensions of therapeutic activity and analytic attention, illustrating fine attunement to changes in therapeutic focus. The symposium presentations revealed the emergence of individual patient/therapist dyads in which organizing theories and ways of relating were uniquely interpreted and expanded. These narratives included patients who had experienced adoption, addiction, immigration, political trauma, partner loss, early pathological sexual activity, and childhood neglect. These unique therapeutic situations are captured in rich detail, with deep candor and authenticity.

For some time, psychoanalysts have been attempting to utilize complex systems theory as a tool to understand their interactions with their patients, as well as their own clinical processes. One of the difficulties in doing so stems from the fact that systems theory seems better at describing what has already happened than it is at predicting what is likely to happen in the future. This article details 3 small elaborations of complex systems theory that may help clinicians utilize it more proactively and prospectively than before.

This article describes a challenging case involving a patient’s pathologically (or unconsciously) accommodating his wife, within a rigidly organized marriage—an affective inflexibility that also led to dyadic constriction. As the author/analyst (a candidate when I wrote the article), in attempting to make clinical use of Brandchaft’s concepts of unconscious accommodation, I found myself stuck in dyadic repetition, my patient apparently more keen on short-term fixes than engaged vulnerability (parallel to the patient’s antidotal use of online pornography, the presenting symptom). I feared I was not only failing the patient, but also my beloved theorist, in unsuccessfully integrating Brandchaft’s theories into the analysis. In the end, however, it was this vexing anxiety and frustration that illuminated my repetitively paternal transference—not only toward the patient, but also the idealized Brandchaft and his theory of accommodation! Understanding these parallel paternal transferences led to my deeper empathic attunement to the patient, similarly organized, rather than the seeking of results that would justify my sufficiency. A Brandchaftian emancipation began to manifest, only after the analyst surrendered concepts of how such process should or ought to proceed. This expanded attunement to the patient’s frustrated (and fraught) yearnings, in turn, relaxed some of his self-protections, as the patient began to believe, gradually, in the possibility of an authentic relational home.

Carola Kaplan   Carola M. Kaplan, Ph.D., Psy.D., is Member, Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis, Los Angeles; and Professor of English Emerita, California State University, Pomona.CONTACT Carola M. Kaplan, Ph.D., Psy.D. carolakaplan938@gmail.com 21919 Altaridge Drive, Topanga, CA 90290.

One of the most intransigent problems I have encountered in my psychoanalytic practice is the apparently unhealable heartbreak experienced by a patient who has been dumped by a romantic partner. As Freud pointed out, the loss of the loved object is devastating because it is experienced as a loss of the most vital part of the self.

My experience with jilted patients has made it clear that the most important response to these seemingly endless litanies of grief is patience. An important resource that I enlist in maintaining patience is imaginative literature, which helps me to find a pattern in therapy sessions, particularly when a patient is dealing with the exigencies of losing romantic love.

Recently, I have been working with a patient I call Gloria, whose live-in lover left her for another woman. Ordinarily feisty and independent, Gloria responded to this loss with an almost complete collapse. In reaction, I found myself overcome by a feeling of helplessness, which puzzled me until I realized that the collapse of this independent woman reminded me of my mother’s descent into incapacitating depression when I was a child.

What helped me to regain perspective was Julian Barnes’ (2011) novel The Sense of an Ending, which brilliantly illustrates the perplexing blindness in romantic love of an otherwise intelligent and self-reflective man. Barnes’ novel helped me to understand my patient’s difficulties in exchanging her idealized portrait of her ex-lover for a more realistic picture of a fallible human being.

Buttressed by the insights into romantic love offered by this and other literary works, I was able to remain steady and patient as Gloria worked through her grief and achieved a greater sense of purpose and selfhood in the process.

Prologue: The Future of Psychoanalysis in Undergraduate Education: An Innovative Collaboration between The Colorado College and The Chicago Psychoanalytic Institute

Marcia Dobson PHD and John Riker PHD

John Riker

John Riker   John H. Riker, Ph.D. jriker@coloradocollege.edu Department of Philosophy, Colorado College, 14 E. Cache la Poudre, Colorado Springs, CO 80903.

For many years, ancient Jewish myth warned against the study of Kabbalah’s mystical writings until one had attained the age of 40. It was thought that such study was inherently dangerous, even life threatening, for the young. In fact, an illustrative Talmudic story is told of 4 rabbis who, through study of Kabbalah, enter the sacred mystical realm of Pardes. One rabbi died immediately upon entering, one became crazy, one became an apostate and left the religion altogether, and only one, the vaunted Rabbi Akiba, survived intact.

In the same vein, for years, exposure to psychoanalytic ideas was thought by the psychoanalytic establishment to be dangerous for young people. Following that mode of thought, psychoanalytic candidates in the early realm of their training were prohibited from participation in advanced conferences and were barred from listening to some case material. Certainly, at that time, it was unthinkable that psychoanalytic ideas could, or even should, be taught at the undergraduate level.

Marcia Dobson and John Riker, both professors at Colorado College, turned that thinking on its head. With uncommon courage they entered psychoanalytic Pardes, exposed the young ones in their charge to notions about unconscious motivation and more, and came out not only unscathed, but celebrated for their pedagogical “bravery” and innovation.

This issue of PI is a celebration of their students and of what John and Marcia have accomplished.

Allen Siegel, M.D.

Associate Editor, Psychoanalytic Inquiry

Call us crazy. At a time when the world and academia seemed to have turned against psychoanalysis, we so fully believed in its fundamental presuppositions that we embarked on a journey to explore astonishing new ways to bring psychoanalysis into the hallowed halls of undergraduate education. The we are Marcia Dobson, a classicist, and John Riker, a philosopher—both professors at Colorado College and married to one another for four decades. Marcia is a daughter of one of the great women pioneers in psychosomatic medicine, Helen Flanders Dunbar, and has a second Ph.D. (which she started after the age of 50) in Clinical Psychology. Along with her continuing to teach Greek language and culture at the college, she also has a small clinical practice. John’s specialty in philosophy is bringing psychoanalysis to bear on the questions of contemporary ethics, opening up original ways to conceive of ethical life in relation to the new concept of human nature that psychoanalysis has discovered.

Chapter 1: Stirring the Pot

Marcia Dobson PHD

Marcia Dobson

Marcia Dobson   Marcia D-S. Dobson, Ph.D., is a Professor of Classics and the Chair of the Psychoanalysis Minor at Colorado College in Colorado Springs, Colorado. She is the author of a number of articles and book chapters in psychoanalysis and the Classics. She is a member of the International Association of Psychoanalytic Self Psychology and a co-chair of APsaA’s Committee on Psychoanalysis and Undergraduate Education.CONTACT Marcia D-S. Dobson, Ph.D. mdobson@coloradocollege.edu 3510 Temple Drive, Colorado Springs, CO 80904.

Allen Siegel’s startling quotation about the Kabbalah, which prefaces this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, brings to sharp focus what appears to be a long-held belief among psychoanalysts that it is neither recommended nor even wise to teach psychoanalysis to the young. Why is this? Is there a prejudice that our students are too naïve or too tender to foist the vagaries of classical drive theory upon them? Or is that they cannot really understand such erudite and shocking material as the workings of unconscious process because they are not yet mature? Is it perhaps that they simply are unprepared to receive and work with psychoanalytic material in a wise and transformational way? What is the problem anyway? And what does it mean, really, to teach this erudite, theoretical material to eighteen to twenty-two year olds? How does one teach it? Are there pitfalls? And what are the benefits?

For me, and I admittedly had a rather peculiar upbringing, psychoanalytic thinking and discourse was dinner-table conversation. My mother, Helen Flanders Dunbar, M.D., was a well-known psychoanalyst who specialized in psychosomatic medicine and was in her full fame as a writer and clinician when I was born. I grew up hearing words like ego, superego, id, and homeostatic equilibrium, as well as listening, at a developmental stage described by Freud as latency, to sometimes quite bizarre conversations at her cocktail parties with other analysts, while I served them hors d’oeuvres. My mother questioned me frequently about the state of my psyche for her own scholarly edification, which sometimes made me feel like a prize guinea pig, but often also proud to be part of the experiment. At any event, my upbringing gave me an early capacity and curiosity for understanding the mysterious theoretical language of psychoanalysis. Later on, as an adolescent, I helped my mother with her research by accompanying her to international conferences and taking notes at sessions she could not attend, in addition to visiting what were then termed insane asylums. I listened to her in our weekend car trips out of Manhattan to our Connecticut home as she dictated her own patient notes (completely anonymous by numbers) to an accompanying secretary. I was delighted by the sparkle in her eye when she made her new discoveries. I loved her and her work and felt much included by her. I was full of questions.

Chapter 2: Why Teach Psychoanalysis to Undergraduates

John Riker PHD

John Riker

John Riker   John H. Riker, Ph.D., is a professor of Philosophy at Colorado College. He is the author of four books interrelating psychoanalysis and philosophy, especially ethics. He is a member of the International Association of Psychoanalytic Self Psychology and a co-chair of APsaA’s Committee on Psychoanalysis and Undergraduate Education.CONTACT John H. Riker Ph.D. jriker@coloradocollege.edu Department of Philosophy, Colorado College, 14 E. Cache la Poudre, Colorado Springs, CO 80903.

Psychoanalysis is often understood as a medical field with set of practitioners using a therapeutic method to access and transform unconscious psychological propensities and structures in patients. As a medical practice, it really has no place in undergraduate education; however, psychoanalysis is also a rich set of ideas about who we are as human beings, how we function, how we fall ill, what we most need, and what kind of psychological dynamics allows us to live most fully. We feel it is crucial for undergraduate students to be able to learn about these ideas, the most important and powerful set of ideas ever conceived to probe the depths of individual psyches.

The undergraduate college years are, for many students, the time when they will think most deeply and critically about who they are, what direction they want to take in life, and what values are most important to them. They are thinking intensely about profession, sex, gender, sexuality, personal identity, how to be an individual, and what makes life worth living. To do this kind of thinking well, they have to have some notion of what it means to be a human being, what we need to function well, what causes us to malfunction, and what, in fact, gives a depth of happiness to the kind of creatures that we are.

Alas, they often have no resources for thinking about these crucial questions other than the concepts and values of the regnant culture, and, to us, these are, at best, devastatingly shallow and, at worst, offer values that can lead to a profound sense of emptiness, quiet desperation, and dismay that characterizes so many of the adults in today’s culture. It seems to us that we all, but especially the young, need deeper, more complex, more truthful ways of grasping our human souls to construct better lives and a better society, one not so prone to the ravages of mental illness, such as is found in mass shootings, domestic violence, homelessness, and the unchecked narcissism of some of our highest social and political leaders.

Chapter 3: The Class at Allen Siegel’s Home

Marcia Dobson PHD and John Riker PHD

John Riker

John Riker   John H. Riker, Ph.D., is a professor of Philosophy at Colorado College. He is the author of four books interrelating psychoanalysis and philosophy, especially ethics. He is a member of the International Association of Psychoanalytic Self Psychology and a co-chair of APsaA’s Committee on Psychoanalysis and Undergraduate Education.John H. Riker, Ph.D jriker@coloradocollege.edu Department of Philosophy, Colorado College, 14 E. Cache la Poudre, Colorado Springs, CO 80903.

Since the inception of the course in 2007, we have met for a Saturday class and barbeque at Allen Siegel’s home in Winnetka. The students take the commuter train from downtown and then walk half a mile to Allen’s modernist style home, set in a lovely copse of trees. The living room, with its cathedral ceiling, is spacious enough to easily accommodate the class. Its interior is graced with award-winning model ships meticulously constructed by Allen. Although it is rare—almost forbidden—to have a Saturday class, the students have never complained because the event is so meaningful for them—a great discussion followed by a lively barbeque.

The impetus for going to Allen’s house and for having a separate chapter on this class is that the students read Allen’s (1996) classic book Heinz Kohut and the Psychology of the Self, almost cover to cover. The class with Allen tends to be our final session on psychoanalytic self psychology and the students are encouraged to ask Allen any questions they have about his book or about self psychology. Allen is willing to become deeply personal about himself and his experiences with Kohut and with his own patients. He appears to birth empathy itself in his immediacy and connection with our students.

What follows is first a statement by Allen about how he teaches the class, and then we include a sampling of the students’ questions to Allen and their accounts of Allen’s responses.

Allen Siegel writes

Summer begins for me when the kids from Colorado College come to Chicago for their month-long sojourn into a living, breathing psychoanalytic community, accompanied by their teachers, Marcia Dobson and John Riker. They come here, to Chicago, in late May and early June and usually with visit me in my home in Winnetka, Illinois midway through the course. I live in a bucolic setting, certainly a much calmer experience than what the students had lived while in the heart of the city. We gather in my informal living room that easily accommodates 20. Late May/early June in Chicago can be cold and when it is, like this year, I light a fire before we begin.

Chapter 3: Neurobiology and Psychoanalysis

Peter Lehman

Peter Lehman

Peter Lehman   Peter Lehman is a senior Molecular Biology major at Colorado College.CONTACT Peter Lehman P_lehman@coloradocollege.edu 2536 N. 85th Street, Wauwatosa, WI 53226-1914.

Freud proposed that much of human behavior is influenced by unconscious process. He described this unconscious as a psychological structure containing socially unacceptable motives, memories, and desires, unwanted in consciousness due to the emotional pain and conflict they produce. He said these thoughts are forced down both consciously and unconsciously through various defensive mechanisms. The questions I ask myself in response to such a dramatic psychoanalytic concept are ones seeking a neurobiological understanding. What is the neural basis for both conscious and unconscious thought? What neural mechanisms underlie their proposed interaction? How do conscious thoughts become unconscious and vice versa? More broadly, how can a neurobiological understanding be helpful in the clinical sphere? Some would argue that neuropsychoanalysis is not helpful and pursuing these questions puts the validity of psychoanalysis in the hands of neuroscientists. However, I strongly believe that one’s subjective experience, although not quantifiable, can be framed in a quantitative lens advantageous to the patient. Thus far, the questions I have proposed have no definitive answer. But, I hope I can begin to understand the fragile network that connects these two historically opposed fields.

Annotated bibliography

Berlin, H. A. (2011). The neural basis of the dynamic unconscious. Neuro-Psychoanalysis, 13(1), 5–31.

It is accepted in neuroscience that lower levels of processing can occur without conscious perception, such as motor reflexes. When you go to the doctor and they hit your knee with a tiny rubber hammer you don’t consciously extend your leg. No matter how hard you focus on not extending your leg, your leg will still extend after being hit. However, the notion that higher levels of mental processing, such as your emotional state, can be produced unconsciously is still controversial in neuroscience. Many experiments with brain lesion patients have been done to try and prove that nonconscious stimuli can, indeed, elicit emotional states. There is a condition known as affective blindsight that causes patients with damage to their primary visual cortex, but intact retino-tectal projections, to perceive visual stimuli without consciously doing so. Experiments with these patients consist of presenting emotional visual stimuli. Once presented with the emotional stimuli, many patients have affective responses in accordance with the stimuli, although denying any conscious awareness of those stimuli. These responses include behavioral responses. For example, patients presented with forced-choice paradigms in conjunction with the visual stimuli have an above-chance discrimination of emotional facial expressions.

Chapter 1: Healing the Healer’s Art: A Letter to My Professors

Rin Gentry

Rin Gentry

Rin Gentry   Rin Gentry graduated magna cum laude from Colorado College in 2019, with distinction in an independently designed major in psychoanalysis, art, and creativity. Rin is currently living, working, and rock climbing in Colorado, with aspirations to move into the psychoanalytic field. CONTACT Rin Gentry katrin.gentry@gmail.com 2 Woodmont Court, Berkeley, CA 94708.

This article seeks to articulate a problem I’ve noticed in the field of psychoanalysis—namely, the problem of closed-mindedness and reluctance to tolerate the coexistence of contradictory truths. I believe this problem is inhibiting the field from reaching its full potential to heal and continue to discover effective methods of healing. I call upon psychoanalysts and students of psychoanalysis to confront their own biases and attempt to open their minds to the possibility that all schools of psychoanalysis (i.e., Freudian, Kleinian, Kohutian, Jungian, etc.), as contradictory as their teachings and methods may seem, teach valid truths and valuable insights, the knowledge of which can only help us to become better healers. Essentially, the more we open our minds and welcome ideas from all subgenres of psychoanalysis, the more tools we have in our toolbox, and the better we will be able to treat our patients. If we insist that one school of psychoanalysis is superior, and reject the validity of differing viewpoints—if we are caught up in pride and the politics of our field, we are ultimately doing ourselves, our colleagues, and our patients a disservice.

Epilogue: The Influence of Neuroscience on Psychoanalysts: A Contemporary Perspective

Fredric Busch MD

Fredric Busch

Fredric Busch   CONTACT Fredric N. Busch, M.D. fnb80@aol.com Weill Cornell Medical College, Columbia University for Psychoanalytic Training and Research, 65 East 76th Street, Suite 1B, New York, NY 10021.

Studies of neuroscience, including those involving the brain, have been an increasing focus of scientific research. Psychoanalysts should welcome information derived from these studies to help elaborate their theories and clinical interventions. Additionally, they should collaborate with neuroscientists, when possible, in the development of further research ideas. An isolationist approach that walls off psychoanalysis from other disciplines may preserve a particular form of psychoanalysis but will ultimately further marginalize our profession. Mark Solms, in his discussion, describes how his productive, though complex, relationship with the neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp, led to an expansion of their thinking about psychoanalytic and neuroscientific ideas. Efforts to engage with other disciplines, such as has occurred with infant observation and psychoanalytic research studies, have drawn interest from practitioners initially dismissive of psychoanalytic treatments. Recent psychoanalytic treatment studies, including those of our group on panic disorder, have included assessments of biomarkers and neuroimaging that have helped elucidate processes that may contribute to positive treatment outcome (for example, Milrod et al., 2016).

The authors and discussants of this issue demonstrate how psychoanalysts can be curious and thoughtful about neuroscientific ideas in ways that enrich, rather than disrupt, their psychoanalytic treatments. Among many questions, these practitioners are particularly curious about how information from the body becomes translated into symbolic terms and how we might better identify aspects of intersubjectivity. Findings in neuroscience have been and will continue to be an important source of information for these and other issues in psychoanalysis, and psychoanalysts, such as those who have written for this issue, will help to identify how these developments can further our analytic work and better relieve our patients’ distress.

Gabriela Mann PHD

Gabriela Mann

Gabriela Mann   Gabriela Mann, Ph.D., is Training Psychoanalyst, Tel Aviv Institute for Contemporary Psychoanalysis and Human Spirit-Psychoanalytic-Buddhist Training Program; Chair, Post-graduate Program in Self Psychology and the Study of Subjectivity, Psychotherapy Program, Sackler School of Medicine, Tel-Aviv University.CONTACT Gabriela Mann, Ph.D. gabriellamann@yahoo.com 80 Hachoresh Street, Kfar Shmarjahu, 46910, Israel.

In this article, I illustrate how virtual reality may promote reclaiming unlived potentialities, unconscious or disavowed. Using Kohut’s concept of the Virtual Self, I suggest that virtual aspects of the self, its potential capability, are unconscious (or unknown) until met by someone or something that promotes their transformation into a conscious state of mind and supports their realization. In this sense, the virtual experiences of the self are drawn from the preconscious. Three vignettes demonstrate the transformative potential of virtual experiences when they are perceived as recognizing, and responsive to, the Self’s needs. Two vignettes are drawn from ancient myths and illuminate how the virtual zone has inspired transformation and expansion of self awareness already in ancient times. A third vignette is presented to illustrate how, at the advent of social media, disavowed and dissociated needs are channeled into cyberspace as communications that are unconsciously geared to reclaim unlived potentialities. Cyber reality converses with conventional reality and, thus, is appreciated as a mode of psychic advance toward a new kind of self consciousness.

While neuropsychoanalysis, as a hybrid discipline, is formally in its third decade of existence, there has been a striking paucity of papers illustrating the clinical applications and relevance of neuroscientific findings for the practicing psychoanalyst. The contributions in this issue illustrate the challenges and possibilities of such an endeavor. Neuroscientific research may strengthen one’s conviction in his/her theoretical orientation, create opportunities for offering ‘neuroscientific interpretations,’ stimulate new ways of thinking or, at its most ambitious, become the basis for a contemporary scientific metapsychology. A part of good science is to see what everyone else can see but think what no one else ever said. [Amos Tversky, cited in Lewis, 2017, p. 230]

Remembrances

Louis Sander first became known to me in the mid-seventies, when he and I participated in a workshop at the Boston Psychoanalytic Society, chaired by Evelyn Schwaber, on narcissism and the self. I had recently completed what was a standard psychoanalytic education at the time, with Kohut’s work just beginning to emerge in the consciousness of the psychoanalytic community. Although I was fully engaged in clinical work, my experience was one of cognitive dissonance in analytic discussions, where the richness of the clinical experience butted up against an impoverished, mechanical theory, with no available means of conceptualizing process outside of the rigid constraints of the classical position. The (implicit) theory guiding my action did not fit with the theory handed down. I was left with tension and uncertainty about how to think about what I was doing in the consulting room. At first I did not grasp that Sander was talking about issues central to psychoanalytic practice or theory, that his work was eye-opening for both the clinician and the psychoanalytic theorist. I did not appreciate the significance of his very different language, a language rooted in biology of living systems thinking.

As a way of thinking about what the therapist is doing, perhaps we could say a nonconscious theory is operating and organizing action. We would call this therapeutic action at the enactive level, not necessarily aligned with the conceptual level. The tension between the two levels was palpable to me. I felt hamstrung. When I was asked shortly after graduating to teach a course on the neuroses in the institute extension division, which then meant hysteria and obsessive-compulsive neuroses, I could describe clinical phenomena but felt the conceptualizations behind the phenomena were impoverished. There was an unrecognized conceptual crisis in the field, captured by John Bowlby saying, “Although psychoanalysis is avowedly a developmental discipline, it is nowhere weaker, I believe, than in its concepts of development” (1981, p. 249).

Louis Sander’s cutting-edge approach drew on infant observation research; nonlinear dynamic systems theories; and current biology, physics, and other hard sciences. From this vantage point, he rethought the psychoanalytic approach to psychic structure, motivation, and therapeutic action. He opened a window for a broad and inclusive relational metapsychology of the highest order, updating Freud’s project of linking psychoanalysis with scientific paradigms. This article offers an account of Sander’s broad and deep integration of psychoanalysis and developmental research.

It is commonly recognized in psychoanalysis that early life events impact the self and relational experiences of patients. John Riker   John H. Riker, Ph.D. jriker@coloradocollege.edu Department of Philosophy, Colorado College, 14 E. Cache la Poudre, Colorado Springs, CO 80903.

What we have tried to present in this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry is an experiment in how psychoanalysis can flourish in undergraduate education. Although psychoanalysis is taught in many venues at colleges and universities, the experiment of a college course being taught at a psychoanalytic institute is, we believe, unique both in the world and the history of psychoanalysis. We hope that the presentation of student responses to the Chicago analysts and some of their papers will provide strong evidence for how meaningful such a course can be for undergraduate students.

However, the teaching of psychoanalysis at the undergraduate level is also vital for the discipline of psychoanalysis itself, for it not only gives an added dimension to the scope and importance of the discipline but provides it with a connection to youth, a connection that, if fostered, could supply vibrant energy and novel ideas to the discipline. However, the main reason to try to foster interconnections between psychoanalytic institutions and undergraduate colleges and universities is that it grants psychoanalysis a profound legitimation, one that it sorely needs, given how it has been attacked and dismissed over the past half century, especially by psychology departments in American universities and colleges. As a counter to this dismissive attack, we have hoped to show how and why the concepts and ideas of psychoanalysis can be and are deeply meaningful for undergraduate students.

The program at Colorado College is exceptional in having psychoanalysis as an organized field of study (the minor) and in exposing students to the living discipline as it is practiced today by contemporary psychoanalysts; however, it is hardly the only place where psychoanalysis is being taught at the undergraduate level. In a recent study conducted by Colorado College psychology major Alexandra Appel (the results of which were published in The American Psychoanalyst, vol. 52, n. 3, fall 2018), we found that a number of the US News and World Report’s top colleges and universities offered a significant number of undergraduate courses that involved psychoanalysis.

Inspired by the work of Louis Sander (2008), this article explores the paradox of the developing individual who is at once singular and self-regulating, as well as systems-embedded and systems-property organized. Stories, narratives, actions over time reveal character, quirks, personal standards, human relational connections, social values, and even universal meanings! Stories do all this and then some, and good ones often cover many of these bases simultaneously. Good stories embody webs of experience that readers and listeners—and therapeutic partners—register on different levels and in different modes often at the same time. Good stories also shake our conventional assumptions and ways of thinking; they may shatter some adamantine shibboleths and open our minds and imaginations to new and future possibilities. These are the good stories, ones that are open to nuance and complexity and change, ones we try to create and cultivate in our analytic relationships. However, there are other stories, not such good ones, fixed and immovable stories, stuck in time and stultifying to growth and development. These are closed stories, and in this article I will explore varieties of therapeutic narratives that close down thinking and emotions, and I’ll speculate on their origins and remediation.

This issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry provides psychoanalytic clinicians an opportunity to explicate how neuroscientific ideas have influenced their theory and practice. In identifying the applicability of neuroscience, psychoanalysts should consider the following questions: What relevant information has been theorized, identified and studied in neuroscience and how might these findings affect psychoanalytic theories and approaches? To what degree can these findings be integrated with psychoanalytic ideas? Do these findings favor certain psychoanalytic approaches in contrast to others (e.g., efforts to symbolize unrepresented states vs. interpretation of unconscious conflict)? What modifications of psychoanalytic theories and techniques or adjunctive and alternative treatments do neuroscientific findings suggest and across what clinical situations? What psychoanalytic theories and approaches have been indicated to be incorrect by neuroscience? How might psychoanalysis inform neuroscientific theories and research?

AIthough it will not be a focus of this issue, it is also important to consider objections to these efforts, which at times have been vehement (Blass & Carmeli, 2007). These criticisms have focused on the notion that psychoanalysis involves a subjective realm in which neuroscience has no place. In the view of these authors, such efforts actually represent a danger to psychoanalysis, as they distract from psychoanalytic approaches or emphasize theories and interventions that are separate from it. Indeed, there are significant benefits and potential risks deriving from these endeavors.

One core benefit is that consideration of neuroscientific findings (and information from other neighboring disciplines) reduces psychoanalytic isolation and the potential for reductionistic mentalism or excessive certainty about our views. Arrogance about the correctness of psychoanalytic theories and approaches has done significant damage to the profession. Neuroscience, from Freud onwards, has a history of affecting psychoanalytic thought and will continue to do so, and it is important to understand how these developments influence our thinking. Neuroscientific findings that substantiate certain psychoanalytic ideas may increase the perceived legitimacy of psychoanalytic approaches. Psychoanalytic ideas, clearly explained, can be useful to other disciplines, potentially expanding theories and directing studies. Finally, findings from other disciplines enable an expansion of therapeutic options that can allow psychoanalysis to work more effectively. The use of psychotropic medication, initially viewed as a danger to psychoanalytic treatments, is an example of such an intervention.

For more than four decades, George Atwood and I have been absorbed in rethinking psychoanalysis as a form of phenomenological inquiry. In the course of this work, I repeatedly made the claim that phenomenology led us inexorably to relationality, but until now I did not offer an explanation of this inexorability. This article offers a cultural-historical account of the origins of relational psychoanalysis. It proposes that the enthusiasm of many in the first generation of relational psychoanalysts emerged from our engagement with the radical cultural and political movements of the 1960s and early 1970s. It features several common dimensions of relational analysis and those movements: the central role of authenticity and recognition; the critique of power and arbitrary authority; the tolerant and even enthusiastic attitude toward spontaneity, experimentation, turbulence and improvisation; the interest in the social and cultural surround at a core level; and an interest in marginalization processes and in a sense, outsider-ness, both as an identity and as a source of personal pain. The article emphasizes core qualities of the innovative Relational sensibility, especially its open, inclusive and integrative spirit.

Our minds operate within the potentialities and limits of certain biologically based systems. Problems in the functioning of these systems, in conjunction with environmental pressures, can lead to psychopathology. A better understanding of these systems through the neuroscientific ideas of Jaak Panksepp and Antonio Damasio informs psychoanalytic conceptions of and approaches to panic disorder and trauma. Of particular relevance are systems that translate somatic states to emotions and symbolized representations, those that identify mental states in self and others, and those involving aggression, anxiety, and attachment. A series of recommendations regarding treatment interventions are made based on these ideas.

Yoram Yovell

Yoram Yovell   Yoram Yovell is a psychiatrist, neuroscientist, and supervising psychoanalyst. He is associate professor of clinical psychiatry at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. He studies the neurobiology of mental pain and its relation to suicidality, with the aim of improving the treatment of suicidal individualsCONTACT Yoram Yovell, M.D., Ph.D. yoram.yovell@mail.huji.ac.il Division of Clinical Neuroscience, Hadassah Ein Kerem Medical Center, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem 91120, Israel.

As Louis Sander understood, human infants are evolutionarily endowed with emotional minds that allow them to experience themselves as affectively vibrant creatures, who seek to be recognized as important players in the world. If so recognized, they experience themselves as positive individuals; if merely neglected as predetermined beings whose affects and intentions do not matter in the long-term construction of their minds, paths toward adult disturbance are paved. The neuroscience of affective processes has been substantively advancing through the use of animal models where the needed detailed experimental work can be conducted. Critical neural networks and neuro-epigenetic brain changes are being documented that provide neuroscientific confirmations for the insights advanced by Sander and his many colleagues. Here we show how the deeply intersubjective, flexible nature of the mother-infant relationship is firmly expressed in the underlying biology of the basic limbic emotional systems. Rather than being deterministic, hard-wired affective switches, these emotional systems (e.g., CARE, PLAY, PANIC, SEEKING, RAGE, FEAR, and LUST) are modulated by (and, in turn, modify) the developing relationship between mother and infant. Thus, the nature-nurture debate can be meaningfully reconceptualized as a bio-psycho-social interactive model, in which biology shapes relationships, which, in turn, shape and sometimes radically modify the biology.

This article contends that psychoanalysis benefits from a neurobiological perspective. It is suggested that Antonio Damasio’s view on the neurobiology of mind and self is particularly useful in this regard. The article presents a review and discussion of Damasio’s basic assumptions on body, emotion, feeling, unconscious and conscious mind, and embodied self. It explains how Freud’s hypotheses that ego is first and foremost a bodily ego is underpinned by contemporary neurobiological research and theory. A clinical illustration highlights that changes in sense of self encompasses changes throughout the whole body, as felt from the inside and as observed from the outside.

In this article, I attempt to engage questions about the momentums of the moments of meeting formulated by Lou Sander as propitious for early development. I wanted to portray observations that grapple with the intersection between psychic change and complex dynamics, like imagistic confluence with verbalized interaction, embodied recognition from parent to child, and affecto/libidinal communication between patient and analyst. The focus is on four different directions for comments: (1) Some links to my own clinical practice and research; (2) An instance of “confluence of visual image between patient and analyst”, a moment of imagistic meeting, as understood through self-analysis by an open-minded analyst, including the discovery of “the importance of unsuccessful empathy in learning and growing”; (3) A study of “engrossment,” exemplifying the ways in which the earliest moments of “recognizing” ones infant, can engender joyful, expansive affects, with enhancement of self-image in fathers; and (4) The continuing generative momentum of Lou Sander’s participation within the Boston Change Process Study Group.

Prologue: The Ubiquity of Unconscious Communication

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein   CONTACT Melvin Bornstein, M.D. melvinbornstein@gmail.com 625 Purdy Street, Birmingham, MI 48009.

Many years ago, shortly after I began psychoanalytic training and my analysis, I conducted a psychodynamic psychotherapy with a depressed young man who experienced traumatic neglect by his mother. As he spoke in boring detail about what appeared to me irrelevant topics, an image of Picasso’s enigmatic painting La Vie frequently flashed into my awareness. La Vie was painted at the beginning of Picasso’s blue period. It is somber. At one side of the canvas is a young man embracing a woman pointing at an intimidating older woman holding a baby.

After some work in my analysis about the loss of my mother’s interest in me because of her mental illness, I turned to my experience with this depressed young man to understand what was taking place in the therapy. I also learned that Picasso painted La Vie after his friend, Casegemus, had killed himself, thinking he had killed the woman he loved, who had recently rejected him. Picasso was extremely mournful and, I imagine, depressed. As I thought about my patient, myself, and Picasso, I developed a better understanding of my patient and the therapeutic process.

As I look back many years at this situation, I was in a very complex state of unconscious communication between my patient, myself, and an intrapsychic object of Picasso. I was immersed in a psychotherapeutic process with my patient, working on components of his depression, while focusing on my depression, which merged with my reaction to Picasso’s La Vie.

I was also unconsciously communicating to my patient that I was trying to understand his depression through parts of my depression, which contributed to the depth of my empathy. I was also showing myself that, through Picasso’s genius, I could see that much more can be done with depression than remaining depressed.

Over the years I have frequently returned to the phenomena of unconscious communication that began in a clinical setting.

When Harriet Pappenheim suggested an issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry devoted to clinical material demonstrating unconscious communication, Joe Lichtenberg and I thought it would be an intriguing issue that will lead further exploration of this area of inquiry.

Epilogue: The Ubiquity of Unconscious Communication

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein   CONTACT Melvin Bornstein, M.D. melvinbornstein@gmail.com 625 Purdy Street, Birmingham, MI 48009.

These articles demonstrate the ubiquity of unconscious communication from isolated situations to an entire analysis. Without the inclusion of unconscious communication, it is not possible to convey the depth and complexity of human experience that is part of every clinical moment.

Sixty years ago, as a freshman medical student, I first heard a lecture by our Psychiatry Professor, John Dorsey. He spoke to the first- and second-year classes once-a-week as an introduction to the human aspects of medicine. For two years, I heard one message from him: Human beings are whole people; they are driven by a love for life. They become ill when they turn away from parts of themselves that they can’t love and put them outside of themselves and then hate those parts. Health is based on the fact that “we are our own everything.” We heard this refrain repeatedly. Now, I did not know what this man was talking about, but I knew he was right. For years, I knew that those words were having a great effect on me and understood this to be unconscious communication.

I devote this epilogue to demonstrate how those words carried through unconscious communication and over many years changed my life. When I was 5 years old, my mother lost interest in me because of her mental illness. She was eventually institutionalized. My father and I moved in with my aunt and uncle. My father eventually moved out, leaving me with them. I would frequently spend time with my father. I became phobic about visiting my mother in the State Hospital. My father remained committed to her, visited her frequently, and encouraged me to visit her. I only occasionally joined him.

Of course, many years of my analysis, self-analysis, and analytic work have been devoted to developing the emotional strength to deal with the complexity of my experience, principally to use my trauma to contribute to the fulfillment and joy of my living which involved learning all I could from the past to develop a capacity to live well in the present.

Over the years, we have been graced with the presence and wisdom of many exceptional Chicago analysts. A number of those who have spoken to the class are either no longer with us or have retired, including Ernest Wolf (on self psychology and empathy), Marian Tolpin, (on the forward edge), Sallie Jenkins (a feminist case study), Kenneth Newman (on D. W. Winnicott), and Arnold Goldberg on multiple case studies exemplifying his work on the vertical split. Arnold Tobin has spoken on classical Freudian analytical theory, primarily sexuality and the structural model of the psyche. Others who have come to our class, but who are also not represented in the responses that follow, include Virginia Berry (Proust and neuroscience), Christine Kieffer (on oedipal victors and child therapy), Denise Davis (a case study on therapeutic boundaries), Robert Galatzer-Levy (chaos theory), Carla Leone (couples therapy), Jonathan Lear (his book Radical Hope [2006] and his work on irony [2011]), Mark Levy and Linda Marino (a comparative theoretical case study), Bonnie Litowitz (gender fluidity), Jane McCormack (a case study), Erika Schmidt (the Chicago Institute, of which she is the present Director), Neal Spira (religion—especially Judaism—and psychoanalysis). It is hard to express how much we learned from these analysts; they were transformative thinkers not only for the class, but for both of us.

The class also spends a full day at the Institute for Clinical Social Work (ICSW), where a number of therapists and analysts have presented, including Alan Levy, Scott Rose, Gabriel Ruiz, Karen Bloomberg, and more who have gathered to discuss the video On Treatment with the students. (The students find themselves interested in ICSW because it is one of the few institutions that offers an initial practicing degree with a concentration in psychoanalysis).

It is, of course, impossible to do a transcription of each of the classes taught by our analysts. What we think is important for a volume devoted to psychoanalysis and undergraduate education is for readers to get a sense of how the students took in what the analysts were saying. These responses in no way should be taken as accurate reports of what the analysts said, but vignettes of how a representative set of students responded to the particular class. We asked students to give both their thoughts about the presenting analyst and something of what they learned. We include these responses because they give a picture of what young people can learn (and not learn!) from the presentations of psychoanalysts.

Rebecca Stine

Rebecca Stine   Rebecca Stine graduated from Colorado College in 2019 with a major in English/Creative Writing and a minor in Psychoanalysis. I find myself at a roadside that is both nowhere and also exactly the place I need to be. It is daytime, but it is gloomy and the sun is hard to see. I stand between a dying tree, and a large stone, and I share this space with my sister. We are waiting for Godot.

As I watch and reflect on the production of Waiting For Godot, I am reminded of one of my last interactions with my sister, Maddie. She is now 22 years old and reaching the end of a year-and-a-half period of time off college in which she has traveled through India, Nepal, Italy, Australia, New Zealand, Indonesia, and the United States. Maddie took that year-and-a-half to find something that would bring her growth, as her 2 years in college had left her with only a few people she called friends, and a deep feeling that she lacked inspiration and passion. Just 2 weeks ago now, we were sitting in a car with our mother and father, driving from a funeral in Baltimore to visit a sick relative in North Carolina. It had been two days past the deadline for Maddie’s next decision. Her year-and-a-half of exploration came with an agreement to make a decision about whether to go back to college and finish her degree, or commit to some other long-term way of life, where she could be more self-sustaining. She chose to continue with and complete her college degree, and this road trip marked the end of a period of several months where she was to decide between the two schools she was accepted to. After at least an hour of weighing the pros and cons, and moving in circles around which school was the better option, Maddie seemed somewhat indifferent to both. My father finally asked her, “So, Maddie, what are you thinking? Where do you want to go to school?” I watched my sister freeze in the back seat, unable to say anything back to my father, and I noticed the way in which we all released heavy sighs. I kept pushing her, “Maddie they’re both great schools, this is about what you want. What do you want, what makes you excited?” But I noticed that the more I asked, and the more I pushed her to come closer to a choice, the quieter she became and the further she retreated from the car space and into her own head.
